# Introduction

**Mass spectrometry (MS)** is a key method in proteomics. It enables high-precision identification, quantification and characterisation of proteins in large scale. 

This tutorial processes publicly available LC-MS/MS data. In this type of experiment, proteins are digested into peptides, separated by liquid chromatography (LC), and analysed in two mass spectrometry stages. Raw spectra are matched against protein database to assign peptide sequences, the peak intensities  are aggregated to protein-level abundances and compiled into an expression matrix. This technique is called label-free quantification (LFQ), because quantification is based on peak intensities and computational techniques rather than isotopic labels. Like RNA-seq, LFQ measures abundance, but for proteins instead of transcripts. 

![Switzar et al., doi:10.1021/pr301201x](data/proteomics/bottom_up_ms.png)

In this tutorial the starting point is the expression matrix. 
 
## Dataset

The dataset comes from the PRIDE database, which contains freely available proteomics datasets. 

* [PRIDE: PXD007826](https://www.ebi.ac.uk/pride/archive/projects/PXD007826)
* Selection criteria:
  - Publicly available 
  - LC-MS/MS, label-free quantification (LFQ)
  - Simple design with parallels to RNA-seq experiments
  - Mouse data
  - Immunology related study from Turku

**Expression matrix**: ProteinGroups.txt is in MaxQuant format and contains both intensities and useful metadata. Rows are protein groups: Proteins indistinguishable by peptide fragments are grouped into protein groups.

**Experimental setup**

[Mohammed *et al.* 2018, Quantitative proteomic characterization and comparison of T helper 17 and induced regulatory T cells](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.2004194) 

* Control: T cell receptor activated helper T cell (Th0)
* Case 1: *in vitro* differentiated Th17 cells
* Case 2:  induced regulatory T (iTreg) cells
* Three biological replicates (different cultures)
* Three technical replicates
* Organism: Mouse

## R Package: DEP2

DEP2 is a relatively new R package for analysing mass spectrometry-based proteomics data. It provides differential expression and enrichment analysis pipelines. It has easy to use functions for visualization and  imputation, but it is not very flexible and cannot handle more complex study designs.  For statistical testing DEP2 calls functions from established omics analysis package [limma (Linear Models for Microarray and Omics Data)](https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/limma.html).  

* [DEP2 Quick start](https://mildpiggy.github.io/DEP2/articles/01_Quick_start.html) 
* [DEP2 Analysis workflow](https://mildpiggy.github.io/DEP2/articles/03_DEP2_analysis.html)


**Alternatives to DEP2:**

* [MSStats](https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/vignettes/MSstats/inst/doc/MSstatsWorkflow.html), R package. More widely used and more flexible, but (in my opinion) more complicated to use. 
* [limma](https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/limma.html), R package. General purpose omics data analysis package, no proteomics specific function. Flexible statistics functions. 
* [Perseus](https://maxquant.net/perseus/), graphical software: Established, no R integration.

**Installation of DEP2**

DEP2 is already installed to course environment. 

```{r DEP2 installation, eval = F}
install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("mildpiggy/DEP2")
```

Load packages

```{r libraries, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
library(tidyverse) 
library(DEP2)      
library(patchwork) # combine ggplot figures
```

Paths

```{r paths}
datadir = "data/proteomics"     # Directory for data
resdir = "results/proteomics"   # Directory for results
prefix = "dep2"                 # Name of the project
```


## Basic protocol for DEP2

DEP2 basic analysis protocol is relatively simple: First expression data is converted to `SummarizedExperiment` object and log transformed. Then data is filtered, normalised and imputed. Finally data can be tested for differential expression and different visualizations can be drawn. 

```{r DEP2_basic_protocol, eval = F}
#DO NOT RUN THIS CODE BLOCK. THE BLOCK ILLUSTRATES OVERALL PROTOCOL.

# 1. Construct SummarizedExperiment object and log transform
uniq_pg <- make_unique(proteinGroups)
columns <- grep("LFQ.intensity.", colnames(uniq_pg))
se <- make_se(uniq_pg, columns, expdesign, log2transform = TRUE)                       

# 2. Filter low quality protein groups
filt <- filter_se(se, thr = 1, filter_formula = ~ Reverse != '+' & Potential.contaminant !="+")

# 3. Normalize
norm <- normalize_vsn(filt)

# 4. Impute missing values, i.e. replace replacing missing data with plausible values.
filt <- DEP2::impute(norm, fun = "QRILC")

# 5. Test for differential expression
diff <- test_diff(filt, type = "control", control = "my_control")
dep <- add_rejections(diff, alpha = 0.01, lfc = 1.5)

# 6. Plot differential expression
plot_volcano(dep)
plot_heatmap(dep)
```

In present tutorial we will also have **an additional averaging step**, because our example data has both *technical* and *biological* replicates, which DEP2 cannot handle explicitly.   

# Pre-processing

## Load the data

Our input data is in MaxQuant format, which is tab a limited table. Rows are protein groups. Columns have both intensities and useful metadata.

```{r load_data}
# Load proteinGroups table
mq_pgfile <- paste0(datadir, "/proteinGroups.txt")
pg <- read.csv(mq_pgfile, sep = "\t", na.strings = c("", "NA"))
```

*Open the table and examine the columns.* 

You can find:

* Protein and gene identifiers
* Variety of protein and peptide properties
* Different intensity measures for all samples
* Data quality measures

*Print all column names using `names` function. Can you find a column for Protein names? What about molecular weight or potential contaminants?*

<details><summary>Column names</summary>

```{r mq_column_names}
# Column names
```
</details><br>


**`LFQ.intensity.*`**  columns contain normalised intensities and are used for analysis. LFQ means label free quantification. End part of the file name defines the sample. 

*Can you guess what different parts in column name "LFQ.intensity..Exp2_Th0_3" refer to?*

Next we clean column names with regular expressions. We switch name of condition before biological replicate and remove extra dots. Purpose is to make DEP2 default figures clearer. *This step is not required*, it is made for clarity.

```{r clean_data}
# For clarity, we will change the order of column names: 
# For example LFQ.intensity.Exp1_Th17_1  -> LFQ.intensity.Th17_Exp1_1 
#          (anything).(Exp and numbers)_(anything exept "_")_(any number)    
colnames(pg) <- sub("^(.*)\\.(Exp\\d+)_([^_]+)_(\\d.*)$", 
                    #change order for 2nd and 3rd parenthesis
                    "\\1.\\3_\\2_\\4", colnames(pg))   
# Replace repeated dots with a one dot.
colnames(pg) <- gsub("\\.+", "\\.", colnames(pg))
```

We will create a unique column for names with build in function from DEP2.

```{r create_name_column} 
# Remove entries with both Gene names and Protein names missing
# 'make_unique' gives an error, if this is not done
pg_uniq <- pg |> filter(!is.na(Gene.names) | !is.na(Protein.IDs))

# Create a new column for unique name: If gene name is missing, use protein id.
pg_uniq <-  make_unique(pg_uniq, "Gene.names", "Protein.IDs", delim = ";")
```


## Convert and transform

DEP2 presents the data as [a SummarizedExperiment object (SE)](https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/vignettes/SummarizedExperiment/inst/doc/SummarizedExperiment.html#anatomy-of-a-summarizedexperiment). SE object is a standardised container for omics data. Wide variety of omics methods uses it as an internal format or can convert to it. Shared format is practical also for multi-omics analysis. SE object has three main parts, **`assay`** (the expression matrix), **`colData`** (information about samples) and **`rowData`** (information about rows). When data is stored as a coherent object instead of several individual tables, data processing and analysis is more efficient and far less error prone. 

*What could go wrong during filtering, if you handled your data as separate tables?*

`DEP2` has a function to convert intensity data from MS experiment to the SE format. `DEP2::make_se_parse()` extracts `assay` and `rowData` from the input table based on regular expression, while `colData` is parsed from the column names. If you prefer to explicitly provide table for `colData`, you can use function `DEP2::make_se()`.

```{r make_se_parse}
# Expression column indexes in the input data
ecols <- grep("LFQ.intensity.*Exp", colnames(pg_uniq))

# Convert to SummarizedExperiment AND TRANSFORM
# Sample names are parsed from column titles
se_all <- make_se_parse(pg_uniq,
                        columns = ecols,      # Select relevant columns
                        mode = "char",        # Column names parsed by number of characters
                        chars = 1,            # Last letter denotes the replicate number
                        log2transform = TRUE) # Transform intensities
se_all
```

*How many proteins and samples we have?*

Function `make_se_parse` performs automatically log2 transformation to intensities. Log transformation is required, because distribution of intensities is heavily skewed to the right.  

*Why can we not perform statistical analyses with highly skewed data?*

*Create a test dataset without log transformation by setting the log2transform option to FALSE, as done previously.*

```{r why_log2, fig.width=10, fig.height=8}
#Let's create an object without transformation
se_not_log_transformed_all <- 

# When table is converted to an SE object, creating plots with DEP2 is straightforward
plot_normalization(se_not_log_transformed_all) / plot_normalization(se_all)

# Plotting function x axis title suggests that transformed intensities
# Images are ggplot objects, so you could manually fix the x axis title if you wish.
```

## Averaging of technical replicates

Our data contains both technical and biological replicates. DEP cannot handle them explicitly. We can, however, average technical replicates using R, if they are similar to each other. Convenient way to evaluate overall similarity of different samples is principal component analysis. 

**PCA plot**

Omics data is high-dimensional, i.e. there is large number of different variables. PCA (Principal Component Analysis) simplifies datasets by transforming correlated variables into fewer uncorrelated principal components (PCs). This helps visualise patterns and identify similar sample clusters.

DEP2 function `plot_pca()` performs PCA and creates a plot for two principal components. You can use this plot to observe whether technical replicates and biological replicates are clustered together and whether samples from different experimental conditions are different. 

*Create PCA plot with function `plot_pca()` using `se_all` as an argument.*

```{r pca_plot, warning=FALSE}
#PCA plot
```

*Consider the following questions:*

* *How clearly are technical and biological replicates clustered in this plot?* 
* *Are cell types different to each other?*
* *Why can we average technical replicates?*
* *What would you do, if one of the replicates did not cluster with other replicates?* 

Alternative to averaging would be to model replicates explicitly, which would not be not possible in `DEP2`, while `limma` can be used for more sophisticated statistical analysis. 

**Average replicates**

We average matrix by hand with R, because DEP2 does not support aggregating columns.

Note that when we ignore NA values (`na.rm = TRUE`), we in fact *imputate*: We assume that missing values are average of other technical replicates for given protein and condition. If all three technical variants are NA's, then NA value is retained.

```{r average_technical}
# Extract expression matrix from the SE object with `assay()` function
mtx <- assay(se_all) 

# Create new names for columns by removing replicate number
col_groups <- str_remove(colnames(mtx), "_\\d+$") |> unique()

# Go through each group and average rows within the group
mtx_avg <- sapply(col_groups, function(x){
  # Find column indices for a given condition 
  cols <- grep(x, colnames(mtx))
  # Take the mean for each row in a given condition
  rowMeans(mtx[,cols], na.rm = T)
}) # sapply automatically combines all rowMean vectors back to a matrix
  
# na.rm creates NaN values, if all are NA. We change them back to NA
mtx_avg[is.nan(mtx_avg)] <- NA  

# We can use mean instead of median, because technical replicates for
# given protein in given condition are likely to be normally distributed
```

Now we need to recreate a SE object. We will use **the averaged matrix as an assay**, we will keep **the same rowData** and we will **manually update the colData** to correspond a new averaged matrix. 

**Read the new column data**

Next we will read updated column data from a file. Now replicates represents biological replicates. Controls (Th0) are divided to two groups, because experiments 1-3 and in experiments 4-6 cluster separately in PCA plot.

```{r read_in_coldata, message=F, warning=F}
expdesign <- read_tsv(paste0(datadir,"/expdesign.tsv"))
expdesign
```
The first column must correspond the column names in the matrix.

```{r show_colnames}
colnames(mtx_avg)
```


**Recreate the SummarizedExperiment object**

This time we will use the constructor from SummarizedExperiment package, not a DEP2's wrapper function. 

*Construct a new object with averaged assay data and newly imported column data.*

```{r se_again}
# Then we recreate the SE object SummarizedExperiment, not with DEP2s wrapper
se <- SummarizedExperiment(
  assays =  ,           # Averaged expression matrix 
  colData = ,           # The updated column data
  rowData = rowData(se_all)   # Original rowData is preserved
)
se
```

*How many proteins and samples we have now?*

**Always avoid these kind of manual changes!!**  

*Why is it better to use build-in functions, if possible?* 


## Filter

The expression matrix may contain low quality proteins, which can introduce noise and bias into the analysis, potentially leading to false positives. In filtering step we will remove such proteins.

Below plots shows number of proteins by sample. "Protein identification overlap plot" illustrates how many proteins were observed in a given number of samples. It can be helpful in finding a suitable threshold for filtering missing values. 


```{r plot_freq, fig.width=10, fig.asp = 0.4 }
plot_numbers(se) + plot_frequency(se) 
```

We will remove protein groups that:

* **Have too much missing data**. We remove protein group more than 75 % of proteins are missing. We also require that there is at least one experimental condition, where there is no more than one missing value. In proteomics, missing values are common and may represent low expression that stays below detection limit. You should adjust these criteria according dataset. 
* **Have potential contaminants** (column "Potential.contaminant"): For example trypsin from digestion or keratin from skin. 
* **Match to decoy proteins** (column "Reverse"): Sequence databases include reverse-sequence proteins that are used as controls in pre-processing. Any protein matching these sequences is likely a false positive.
* **Are identified by single modified peptide** (column "Only.identified.by.site"). Such identifications are often unreliable.

```{r filter}
se_filt <- filter_se(se, 
                     #Filter unless there exists at least one condition where there is no more than one missing value
                     thr = 1,  
                      # Minimum fraction of non-missing values in the whole row 
                     fraction = 0.25,
                     #filter out other bad values 
                     filter_formula = ~ is.na(Reverse) & is.na(Potential.contaminant) & is.na(Only.identified.by.site)
                     )
se_filt
```

*How many protein groups did we remove?*


*Redraw "Proteins per sample" and "Protein identifications overlap" plots for filtered data* 

```{r plot_freq2, fig.width=10, fig.asp = 0.4}
# Proteins per sample and identifications overlap for **filtered** data
```

*How would you interpret these images?*

## Normalisaton

**Variance stabilising normalisation**

DEP2 uses variance stabilising normalisation for normalising the proteomics data. The basic idea is that it 1. converts data to approximately *normal distribution* and *stabilises variance* across intensity ranges. This ensures normality and homoscedasticity (similar variance), which many statistical tests assume. VSN normalisation has performed well in a comparison study [Välikangas *et al.*](https://academic.oup.com/bib/article/19/1/1/2562889). 

```{r normalize, message=FALSE}
# Normalize the data
se_norm <- normalize_vsn(se_filt)

# Plot standard deviation vs. mean. If line is horizontal, variance does not depend on mean
# meanSdPlot(assay(se_norm))  
```

Plot the distribution before and after normalisation. 

```{r normalize_plots, fig.width=10, fig.height=6}
plot_normalization(se_filt, se_norm)
```

*Do you see differences between the plots? Should you be concerned?*


**Alternative normalisation methods**

There are also other normalisation techniques. Common techniques are **median normalisation** and **quantile normalisation**. Median normalisation  *shifts intensities to the common median*, but does not change the shape of distributions. Quantile normalisation forces samples to *similar distribution by aligning quantiles*. Both of these methods primarily correct for the batch effect, but do not force normal distribution. 

Check the following links for more information. In `DEP2` this requires conversion to `Qfeature` object. 

* [Normalisation of QFeature object in DEP2](https://mildpiggy.github.io/DEP2/reference/normalise_pe.html)
* [QFeature package](https://rformassspectrometry.github.io/QFeatures/index.html)

**Save your progress**

Let's save our normalised SE object so that we can read in at the beginning of next lecture and we do not rerun everything.

```{r save_rds}
saveRDS(se_norm, str_glue("{resdir}/{prefix}_norm.Rds"))
```


Read in the normalised SE object.

```{r read_rds}
se_norm <- readRDS(str_glue("{resdir}/{prefix}_norm.Rds"))
```


## Imputation

Proteomics results based on mass spectrometry often have large fraction of missing data and imputation is necessary. Imputation is the process of estimating and replacing missing data with predicted values. First we will take a deeper look at different types of missing values and their imputation.

### Types of missing data

There are three principal types of missing values:

| **Mechanism** | **Name**                      | **Depends On**     | **Example in Proteomics**                    | **Typical methods**                  |
|:--------------|:------------------------------|:-------------------|:---------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------|
| **MCAR**      | Missing Completely At Random  | Nothing            | Random instrument noise                      | Mean, median                         |  
| **MAR**       | Missing At Random             | Observed data      | Inferring values from co-expression patterns | Machine learning, statistical models |
| **MNAR**      | Missing Not At Random         | Unobserved data    | Low-abundance peptides undetected            | Left-censored                        |

Different types of missing data require different imputation strategies. If data is **missing completely at random**, simple average might be enough: When we took averages of technical replicates and ignored missing values, we in practice did impute with the average.  However, expression patterns of proteins are correlated within themselves and we can assume, that missing values are behaving similarly to other co-expressed proteins. Such data is **missing at random**. Machine learning-based methods and sophisticated statistical models can capture complex relationships between variables and are well suited for imputing MAR. On the other hand, missing values in mass spectroscopy often represents values that are **below detection limit**, i.e., they are **missing not at random**. For such cases, common approach is to replace missing values with small values that are below the detection limit. These are called left-censored methods. Real life data has is often a **mixture** of different types of missing values and selecting best approach is not always trivial. 

*Let us look the patterns of missing values in our dataset:* 

* *Are there any patterns? Are missing values clustered to particular samples and proteins?* 
* *Are some of the missing values scattered evenly to different samples?*

```{r missin_plot2, fig.asp=1}
plot_missval(se_norm)
```

Plot below divides all proteins to two groups, to proteins with some missing values and proteins with complete data. We can see that missing values are biased to lower intensity protein, which indicates MNAR. 

```{r missing_distribution}
plot_detect(se_norm)
```

### Imputation methods

**Left-censored methods**

The simplest way to impute values below detection level is **zero imputation**: If protein is not detected, there is no protein. However, this produces very unrealistic intensity distributions, **inflating fold changes**. Slightly more realistic method is **minimum imputation**, where smallest value of each protein is used for imputation, but also this results bimodal intensity distribution (= two peaks). **Avoid zero or minimum imputation!**

**MinProb** and **QRILC** use intensity distribution to more realistically model missing values near detection limit. MinProb is more commonly used, while QRILC performs well in a comparison study [Wei *et al.*](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-017-19120-0) and is a default in DEP2. Also, Gaussian imputation from software Perseus is based on similar principles. These methods are good options for imputing MNAR data. 

```{r imputation_mnar, fig.asp = 1.25, message=FALSE}
se_imp_zero <- DEP2::impute(se_norm, fun = "zero")
se_imp_min <- DEP2::impute(se_norm, fun = "min")
se_imp_minprob <- DEP2::impute(se_norm, fun = "MinProb")
se_imp_qrilc <- DEP2::impute(se_norm, fun = "QRIL")
plot_imputation(se_norm, se_imp_zero, se_imp_min, se_imp_minprob, se_imp_qrilc)
```

**Local patterns by machine learning**

Real data has a mixture of different types of missing values.  Machine learning algorithms take advantage of co-expression patterns and can capture complex non-linear dependences. **MissForest** uses so called **random forest** classifier and has performed well in comparison studies [Harris *et al.*](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jproteome.3c00205), [Jin *et al.*](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7815892/). However, MissForest is slow for large datasets. A faster alternative is clustering algorithm **kNN**.   

*Impute with random forest classifier (option "RF") and plot imputation for `se_norm` and `se_imp_RF`*

```{r imputation_rf, fig.asp=0.5, message=FALSE}
# Plot distribution before and after random forest imputation
se_imp_rf <- 
```

**No imputation**

Imputation can cause bias in results. You should consider how relevant missing values are for your biological question. Find out how much missing values there are and what type are they likely to represent. Also non-imputed data can work well [Harris *et al.*](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jproteome.3c00205).

You may perform **a sensitivity analysis**, i.e. you can test whether choice of imputation method has substantial effect to your results. 

In this tutorial we will proceed with random forest imputation. 

# Analysis

`DEP2` uses [**limma**](https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/limma.html) (Linear Models for Microarray and Omics Data) to test for differential expression. Limma was originally built for microarray data, but can be used also for the proteomics analysis. First limma runs **a linear regression model** for each protein (`limma::lmFit`). Linear model fits a straight line to the data. The slope of the fitted line represents the fold change for the given protein. Linear model is more flexible than for example t-test, because you can add additional covariates to the model. After running linear model, limma uses so called **empirical Bayesian methods** to stabilise variance (`limma::eBayes`). This improves statistical power and provides more stable results when the number of samples is small. 

Assumptions:

* Linear model: Continuous outcome, linearity, normality of residuals, homoscedasticity (similar variance) -> Perform log2 transformation and normalisation steps.
* Linear model: Independence -> Don't mix up technical and biological replicates.
* Empirical Bayesian model: Variance depends on intensity similarly in different proteins.

If you have not performed imputation, limma will exclude missing values from the test. If all values from a group are missing, then whole protein is excluded from the analysis. 


## Differential expression

We will use DEP2's wrapper function for limma `DEP2::test_diff`. This function is built only for simple designs. If you need more complex formula, consider using limma directly. We will use to contrasts: Th17.1 vs. Th0.1 and iTreg.2 vs Th0.2.

*Run ?test_diff to explore additional options* 

```{r}
tests <- c("Th17.1_vs_Th0.1", "iTreg.2_vs_Th0.2")
data_diff <- test_diff(se_imp_rf, type = "manual", test = tests)
```

Extract results table and save it to file. 

*We also extract significant results using cut-offs of 0.01 for the adjusted P-value and 1.5 for the log₂ fold change. Please add correct cut-offs.*

```{r}

# Mark significant hits. We use stringent criteria.
dep <- add_rejections(data_diff, alpha = , lfc = )

# Select rowData and streamline the data frame
results_df <- rowData(dep) |> 
  as.data.frame()  |>
  #Remove unnecessary columns
  dplyr::select(-contains("eptides"), -contains("Identification.type"), 
         -contains("coverage"), -contains("MS.MS"), -contains("ntensity"))

# Select significant hits              
results_sign <- results_df |> filter(significant) 

# Write tables as tsv and excel format.
write_tsv(results_sign, str_glue("{resdir}/{prefix}_sign.tsv"))
write_tsv(results_df, str_glue("{resdir}/{prefix}.tsv"))
writexl::write_xlsx(results_df, str_glue("{resdir}/{prefix}.xlsx"))
```

The differential expression is measured in log2 fold change, because the data is log2 transformed. Zero represents no difference, 1 represents double expression and -2 represents expression that is one quarter of the reference sample.

Let's look five proteins with highest log fold change when iTreg cells are compared to Th0 cells. For clarity we include only a subset of columns. 

```{r}
results_df |>
  dplyr::select(Protein.IDs, contains("iTreg.2_vs_Th0.2")) |> 
  slice_max(iTreg.2_vs_Th0.2_diff, n=5)
```

*Which protein has the biggest log fold change? How many times higher is the expression level? What is adjusted P value for it? Is this a significant hit? Why?*  

*Examine the `results_df` table. Can you find protein Satb1? In which experiment is it differentially expressed? Find log2 fold change, confidence intervals and adjusted p-value for it. How many times larger/smaller is the expression?*

### Plots

**Volcano plots**

In volcano plot, unadjusted P values are plotted as a function of log fold changes and highlighted based on adjusted P values. This results in a shape reminiscent of volcanic eruption, where significant points are scattered near top left (down regulated) and top right (up regulated) corners.

```{r volcano_plot, fig.width=10, fig.height=5, warning=FALSE}
p1 <- plot_volcano(dep, contrast ="Th17.1_vs_Th0.1")
p2 <- plot_volcano(dep, contrast ="iTreg.2_vs_Th0.2")                    
p <- p1 + p2 

ggsave(str_glue("{resdir}/figs/{prefix}_volcano.png"), width = 10, height = 5)
p
```

*Check the volcano plot in the original publication. How similar are the results? Why are the results not identical?*

**Heatmap**

A heatmap is a color-coded matrix that shows data values as colours. Here we have selected only significant proteins and show downregulated genes as blue and upregulated genes as red. We cluster similar samples and proteins together. `DEP2::plot_heatmap` calls functions from the package `ComplexHeatmap`. 


```{r heatmap, fig.asp=1.5, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
# Create a heatmap
ht <- plot_heatmap(dep, show_row_names = TRUE, 
                  indicate = c("condition", "replicate"))

# Figure is NOT in ggplot format, so we need an external function for saving the image.
pdf(str_glue("{resdir}/figs/{prefix}_heatmap.pdf"), width = 6, height = 12)  # Open device
ComplexHeatmap::draw(ht, heatmap_legend_side = "right")      # Draw heatmap
dev.off()   
```

*What patterns do you observe?*

*Rerun the differential expression without imputation and/or using another imputation method and see how volcano plot and heatmap change.*
